description: SpinDrift is health-monitoring software for astronauts built on four real quantum sensors: an OPM magnetometer for the brain, an NV-diamond magnetometer for the heart, a quantum-dot sensor for renin in the blood, and a carbon-dot microneedle patch for bilirubin in the skin. Every reading is checked in Lean against the real conditions where the crew is, from the ISS to the Moon and Mars.
summary: SpinDrift is a crew-health console built around four real quantum sensors: an optically pumped magnetometer (QuSpin QZFM) for brain and heart fields, NV-diamond magnetometers for the heart, a quantum-dot renin nanosensor for blood, and a carbon-dot microneedle patch for skin bilirubin. A full-body 3D twin carries each sensor at true size, and the user can zoom from the whole body through cells, genes and molecules down to the sub-nanometre quantum physics each sensor relies on. Every value is real and sourced: NASA OSDR Inspiration4 crew blood chemistry, live space-weather and geomagnetic feeds for the ISS, published Apollo and InSight fields for the Moon and Mars, real OPM heart and brain recordings, and NV, quantum-dot and carbon-dot lab data. Each real run adds sourced facts to one combined sensor. The sensor equations are machine-checked in Lean 4 and cross-checked in Wolfram, and Lean decides whether each sensor can measure its signal under the user's chosen conditions; missing data is reported as "need more information", never guessed. Deep-space crews need compact, non-invasive monitoring without cryogenics. SpinDrift shows, with verified math, what these sensors can and cannot measure in each mission environment. Not diagnostic.
details:
What it does and how it works

SpinDrift is a crew-health console for deep-space missions built around four real quantum sensors:

  • QuSpin QZFM Gen-3 optically pumped magnetometer (OPM): brain and heart magnetic fields.
  • NV-diamond magnetometers: the heart, using three published builds (JGU, ZAQuant, Q.ANT).
  • Quantum-dot renin nanosensor: blood (Long et al. 2012).
  • Carbon-dot microneedle patch: skin bilirubin (Tabatabaee et al. 2024).

The main page is a full-body 3D twin carrying every sensor at true size, plus one card with four real readouts:

  • A 1,295.9 fT evoked brain field from a real OPM recording.
  • A 5.24 pT heart Q wave from 47 averaged real heartbeats (Kiel Cardio Database).
  • The renin sensor’s 25 pM detection limit.
  • Inspiration4 crew total bilirubin, 0.8 mg/dL (NASA OSDR OSD-575).

Users choose a mission location (ISS, Lunar Gateway, lunar base, Mars transit, Mars surface) and enter conditions: shielding, heartbeats averaged, required signal-to-noise, bandwidth, and renin or bilirubin levels. A checker written in the Lean 4 theorem prover then gives one of three verdicts per sensor: requirements met, not met, or need more information. The sensors on the body glow with that verdict. For example, with 47 averaged beats and a required signal-to-noise of 5, Lean finds that the ZAQuant NV build resolves the heartbeat’s R-peak while the JGU and Q.ANT builds do not.

The ambient field comes from live feeds: the NOAA L1 magnetometer, GOES proton flux, ISS position with the IGRF-14 field model, and NASA ISS Live cabin telemetry. For the Moon and Mars it uses the Apollo 12 (38 nT) and InSight (2,013 nT) surface fields.

Users can zoom from the whole body through cells, genes and molecules down to the sub-nanometre quantum physics:

  • the NV centre in the diamond lattice
  • rubidium spin polarisation
  • quantum-dot energy transfer (FRET)
  • carbon-dot fluorescence

Each sensor has its own tab:

  • 3D model: a rotatable, zoomable model that draws only parts with documented dimensions.
  • Live physics, NV: spin levels and a resonance sweep over a real measured spectrum, plus calls to the ODMR-Lab online simulator from the app.
  • Live physics, OPM: spin dynamics from the Bloch equations.
  • Live physics, quantum dot: a FRET probe you can “cut” like renin does.

Each “real run” processes the next real recording and data rows and adds sourced facts to one combined sensor that only ever grows.

Benefits

  • Shows, with machine-checked math, what each quantum sensor can and cannot measure in each mission environment, and what it would take (shielding, averaging) to get there.
  • These sensors are compact and need no cryogenics. SpinDrift lets you compare all four sensing approaches in one place.
  • Every number carries its source, a tag (live, recorded, calculated, simulated) and a status (verified, to confirm, not stated). Missing data is flagged, never guessed.

Intended impact

Help mission planners, researchers and students judge which quantum sensors are worth testing for crew health beyond low Earth orbit. It turns cutting-edge quantum physics into a tool that links each measurement to the biology it reads. It also offers a model for health dashboards where every value is traceable and the logic is formally verified.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python 3.12, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Lean 4 (v4.35.0), Wolfram Language.
    • App: FastAPI and uvicorn (server), three.js (3D).
    • Data processing: NumPy and SciPy, MNE-Python, ppigrf (IGRF-14), viresclient (ESA Swarm), the Lightstreamer client (ISS Live), colour-science (CIE 1931 colours).
    • Simulation: Qiskit Aer (12 Ramsey circuits run through the coda simulator), ODMR-Lab (NV simulator on Hugging Face).
    • NASA OSDR, NASA Human Research Program
    • NOAA SWPC, ESA Swarm
    • PhysioNet, MNE, OpenNeuro
    • Zenodo, figshare, Mendeley
    • RCSB PDB, UniProt, PubChem, ChEMBL, Open Targets
  • Hardware: no physical sensor is connected. The app models the published specifications of real hardware (QuSpin QZFM Gen-3, the three NV builds, the quantum-dot–Cy5 probe with TIRF readout, the carbon-dot microneedle patch and its IoT reader), and has an ingest endpoint ready for a real instrument.
  • AI assistance: code was written with AI coding assistants (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex), and every value was checked against its source.

How it’s creative

  • A formal theorem prover decides health-sensor verdicts. 50 Lean theorems use only standard axioms and contain no unproven steps, and 10 Wolfram checks confirm the equations.
  • Colour is physics, not decoration. Each sensor’s colour is computed from its actual wavelength with the CIE 1931 tables: the rubidium 795 nm and NV 695 nm lines render spectral red, and the carbon dots’ 439 nm emission renders violet. Colour never means healthy or unhealthy.
  • A powers-of-ten zoom from the body to the quantum level, and a combined sensor that grows only from real runs, like building a tower from real bricks.
  • The NV sensing principle is replayed as a quantum circuit, linking quantum sensing to quantum computing.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: real data only, everything sourced and labelled, clearly not diagnostic.
  • Crew privacy: only openly released, processed NASA data; no attempt to identify anyone.
  • The space environment: the magnetic field varies hugely, from about 42,000 nT at ISS altitude to 38 nT on the Moon. That is roughly 800 times what the OPM’s 50 nT on-board coils can null. Radiation and cabin conditions were also considered.
  • Practicality: power, size and cooling taken from datasheets. No public live feed exists from these sensors on a human in space, and the app says so.
  • Licensing: open data (CC BY and CC0) with attribution in the app’s Sources panel.
  • Robustness: works from saved data if the server is offline.
